answerEvidence.summary: The September 1 notice recommends a full antivirus scan on demand and retains automatic antivirus-stack capabilities. The independent Office 365 article still documents Plan 2 AIR, so that workflow is retained.

distractorEvidence.summary: The dated notice removes manual standalone Endpoint investigations, while the separately retrieved Office 365 Plan 2 article continues its AIR workflow; the option reverses those lifecycles.
An Endpoint-specific retirement notice cannot establish retirement of Office 365 AIR, whose current product article still documents investigations and supported triggers.
The notice expressly retains detection and response in the antivirus stack and recommends on-demand full scans; it does not remove scanning.

rubric.notes: alignment (2/2): Directly tests current automated investigation and response management. accuracy (2/2): Applies the dated notice over contradictory older instructions and keeps workloads separate. scenarioCompleteness (2/2): September 2026 and Office Plan 2 are explicit; this is a runbook revision rather than an unbounded device procedure. distractorPlausibility (2/2): Retired-experience versus retired-capability and cross-workload retirement are credible mistakes. answerUniqueness (2/2): Only c honors both retrieved product contracts. documentationStrength (2/2): Two actual raw product receipts support the lifecycle distinction, notwithstanding the separate schema blocker. difficultyAuthenticity (2/2): Intermediate lifecycle interpretation is appropriate. explanationQuality (2/2): Explicitly warns against treating stale lower-page instructions as current. originality (2/2): Does not repeat existing pending-action approval or device-scan action-selection questions. clarityAccessibility (2/2): Distinct product names and date make the scope clear.

answerEvidence.summary: The AIR flow explicitly says an investigation is not triggered when the designated default alert is disabled or replaced with a custom alert. Restoring that enabled built-in trigger addresses this precise gap.

distractorEvidence.summary: A replacement custom alert remains a custom alert regardless of display name. The source excludes the replacement trigger path rather than using a name-matching contract.
Changing the replacement's severity does not remove the documented exclusion for custom-replaced built-in AIR alerts.
Endpoint device-group remediation settings govern Endpoint response behavior. They do not recreate the disabled Office 365 built-in alert trigger required by the AIR flow.

rubric.notes: alignment (2/2): Investigates configuration of Office 365 automated investigation triggers. accuracy (2/2): Restricts the exclusion to a replaced built-in trigger path, not every possible manual AIR initiation. scenarioCompleteness (2/2): License, audit logging and the previously valid built-in trigger are supplied. distractorPlausibility (1/2): Severity inheritance is plausible; display-name copying and Endpoint group settings are weaker. answerUniqueness (2/2): Only restoration of the actual enabled trigger repairs the stated missing path. documentationStrength (2/2): The raw Office AIR flow explicitly names disabled and replaced alerts; the Endpoint source distinguishes remediation settings. difficultyAuthenticity (1/2): The broken default-policy replacement is announced in the stem, so the solution is closer to intermediate recall. explanationQuality (2/2): Does not claim manual initiation or all custom-detection actions are globally impossible. originality (2/2): Distinct from approving an already-pending remediation and from Endpoint retirement. clarityAccessibility (2/2): The negative observation is a symptom, not a double-negative question.

answerEvidence.summary: The targeted-subscription section explicitly tells the operator to enable read existing events to collect existing records. Here the matching 13:00 records remain locally, access and the query are satisfied, and the choice occurs before the first receipt with no bookmark. Those conditions make initial historical collection supported without asserting any reset of a previously advanced subscription.

distractorEvidence.summary: Minimize latency changes how quickly selected events are delivered; the receipt gives it a short batch timeout. Keeping read existing events at its default leaves selection starting with events generated after first receipt. Faster delivery cannot select the retained 13:00 records that precede the 14:00 receipt.

The progress section defines a heartbeat as an indication that the source is active, including when it has no events to send. Reducing that interval increases activity reporting frequency, not the temporal selection range. Leaving historical reading at the default still omits these pre-receipt records.

Collector-initiated configuration specifies which clients the collector reads and requires appropriate access to their logs. It changes initiation and source targeting, not the separately documented existing-event selection setting. With that setting left at its default, merely choosing this collection model does not include the requested retained history.

rubric.notes: alignment=2: Selecting history for Windows Security event forwarding directly maps to the guide's WEF planning/configuration subskill. accuracy=2: Read-existing is applied before initial receipt, not as a post-delivery replay command; the distinctions from delivery timing, heartbeat and initiation match the receipt. scenarioCompleteness=2: Retention, matching query, access, connectivity, no delivered events and no host/subscription bookmark explicitly remove the previous material state uncertainty. distractorPlausibility=1: Latency, heartbeat and collector initiation are actual controls that an operator might confuse with collection scope, but repeating that historical reading stays at default in every wrong option makes them less discriminating. answerUniqueness=2: Only enabling existing-event reading changes the relevant initial selection boundary; no advanced bookmark now needs resetting. documentationStrength=2: The targeted-subscription, progress, delivery and push/pull sections support every semantic distinction. This score rates actual evidence, not the separately failing Windows URL schema. difficultyAuthenticity=2: Intermediate fits a bounded initial configuration decision that distinguishes what is collected from how it is delivered, without claiming advanced replay troubleshooting. explanationQuality=2: The explanation names the default and first-receipt boundary, and the deeper text expressly excludes bookmark rewind and lost-event recovery. originality=2: This is historical selection, not adjacent sc200-061's absent source auditing; it does not duplicate the installed AMA/CEF concepts. clarityAccessibility=2: Explicit 13:00/14:00 ordering and the named host/subscription pair make the temporal and pronoun referents clear; the absolute no-bookmark condition is a supplied scenario fact, not a universal product claim.

answerEvidence.summary: WEF can only query existing generated events and cannot enable channels or adjust audit policy. Configuring those source-side prerequisites separately and then verifying new records addresses the actual failure despite healthy heartbeats.

distractorEvidence.summary: The article defines historical forwarding as reading existing local records. Here required auditing and the channel were disabled, so previously unrecorded activity is not an existing record for WEF to retrieve.

Collector log capacity affects storage on the collector, while the documented source event-channel enablement is separately configured on clients. Increasing WEC storage does not activate their disabled channels.
Targeted subscriptions restrict which hosts and events are collected. They retain WEF's passive behavior and do not acquire authority to enable audit-policy event generation on source devices.

rubric.notes: alignment (2/2): Direct WEF source-configuration prerequisite within the objective map. accuracy (2/2): Passivity and heartbeat limitations match the implementation receipt. scenarioCompleteness (2/2): Disabled auditing and channel are explicit; the query is already correct. distractorPlausibility (1/2): Historical reconstruction and collector-size remedies are relatively easy eliminations. answerUniqueness (2/2): Only a remedies the missing event generation. documentationStrength (2/2): The receipt explicitly enumerates what WEF cannot configure. difficultyAuthenticity (1/2): Advanced is generous once both missing source settings are supplied. explanationQuality (2/2): Distinguishes participation from actual generated evidence without promising recovery. originality (2/2): Source generation is independent of 060's retained-history selection. clarityAccessibility (2/2): Source hosts, collector and subscription are consistently distinguished.

answerEvidence.summary: The sensitive-data limitations exclude SensitiveType searching of Exchange mailbox data at rest and expressly extend that exclusion to Teams messages stored in mailboxes. The stem is confined to those locations, so the missing hits cannot establish data absence even with a valid custom-type identifier.

distractorEvidence.summary: This option requires replacing the GUID with a name. The custom-type GUID example independently disproves that requirement. Later passages allowing custom names do not invalidate GUIDs, and the earlier ID-only passage conflicts with those later passages. Neither interpretation is needed to reject this name-instead-of-GUID claim.

Searchable sensitive data types describes searching classified SharePoint and OneDrive documents, while the limitations exclude Exchange data at rest. Saying that only Exchange is supported reverses both sides of the documented property/location boundary.

The mailbox limitation explicitly names Teams 1:1 chats, group chats and channel conversations because that message content is stored in mailboxes. The question concerns those compliance messages, not files attached through Teams. Their records are not searched as SharePoint site documents instead of mailbox content.

rubric.notes: alignment=2: Interpreting a misleading eDiscovery content search result is directly within the current Purview eDiscovery investigation subskill. accuracy=2: The repaired text states supported GUID use and the Exchange-at-rest exclusion without turning the source's conflicting custom-name advice into a claim. scenarioCompleteness=2: The valid custom GUID, mailbox-only scope and known matching message isolate a documented property/location limitation rather than an unspecified spelling or content-location error. distractorPlausibility=2: Confusing identifiers, reversing service support and confusing Teams message records with site-hosted content are genuine investigation mistakes, not nonexistent controls. answerUniqueness=2: The mailbox exclusion alone prevents the proposed inference of absence; GUID validity defeats b regardless of the unresolved question of name support. documentationStrength=2: The exact GUID example, site-search description and explicit Teams-inclusive mailbox limitation support all authored claims. Conflicting name guidance remains acknowledged and unused, and this score does not waive the Purview URL schema. difficultyAuthenticity=2: Intermediate suits diagnosis of an unsupported search-property/workload combination after an apparently valid identifier has been supplied. explanationQuality=2: The deeper text explains why a valid identifier cannot remove a location restriction, while b's rationale now carefully avoids the earlier ID-only overstatement. originality=2: The sensitive-type/mailbox fact is different from other eDiscovery case-sensitivity and keyword behavior and from the canonical thirty; the stable concept was not renamed to evade comparison. clarityAccessibility=2: Email, Teams compliance messages, mailbox scope and the no-hit inference are explicit; the longer correct option conveys the necessary limitation rather than adding irrelevant detail, and pronoun referents are clear.
